content:
Winter in the UK presents a particular challenge for the millions of people living with arthritis. Shorter days, cold temperatures, icy conditions and the natural inclination to hibernate on the sofa can cause physical activity levels to plummet — yet staying active during winter is arguably more important than at any other time of year. Regular movement keeps joints lubricated, muscles strong, weight in check and mood elevated. This guide provides practical strategies for maintaining an active lifestyle throughout the British winter.

Quick answer: In winter, all adults in the UK should take a daily 10-microgram (400 IU) vitamin D supplement, as recommended by Public Health England. This is because between October and March, the UK does not receive enough sunlight for the body to produce sufficient vitamin D, which is vital for bone health, immune function, and may help reduce arthritis inflammation.

Why Winter Activity Matters More

The temptation to rest during cold weather is understandable, but inactivity creates a vicious cycle: less movement leads to stiffer joints, weaker muscles, weight gain and lower mood — all of which worsen arthritis symptoms. Research shows that physical activity levels in the UK drop by 20–30% during winter months, and this decline is even more pronounced among people with chronic pain conditions.

Conversely, maintaining activity through winter helps keep synovial fluid flowing (the joint's natural lubricant), prevent deconditioning and muscle loss, support mental health (combating seasonal affective disorder), maintain a healthy weight through the calorie-dense festive season, and reduce the severity and duration of morning stiffness.

Indoor Exercise Options

When outdoor conditions are poor, having indoor alternatives is essential.

Swimming and Aquatic Exercise

Indoor heated pools offer one of the best exercise environments for arthritis in winter. Warm water (typically 28–32°C) soothes joints, provides buoyancy that reduces weight-bearing stress by up to 90%, and allows movement that would be painful on land. Most UK leisure centres have heated indoor pools. Look for "aquafit" or "gentle aqua" classes specifically suited to people with joint conditions.

Home-Based Exercises

  • Chair-based exercises — Full-body workout from the comfort of your living room. NHS and Versus Arthritis have free YouTube videos
  • Yoga and tai chi — Online classes allow you to practice in a warm home environment
  • Resistance band exercises — Compact, affordable equipment for strength training at home
  • Stationary cycling — Pedal exercisers (from £20) sit on the floor and can be used from a chair
  • Stair exercises — If you have stairs, gentle step-ups using the bottom step provide excellent leg strengthening

Indoor Walking

  • Shopping centres — many open early for "mall walking" groups
  • Indoor athletics tracks (some leisure centres have these)
  • Walking on the spot or marching in place while watching television
  • Indoor walking videos on YouTube (Leslie Sansone's "Walk at Home" series is popular)

Exercising Outdoors Safely

If you prefer outdoor exercise, preparation is key:

Layering for Arthritis

  • Base layer — Moisture-wicking thermal underwear keeps skin dry
  • Middle layer — Fleece or wool for insulation
  • Outer layer — Windproof and waterproof jacket
  • Extremities — Thermal gloves (or arthritis compression gloves under warm gloves), warm hat, thermal socks. Heat loss through the head and hands significantly affects comfort
  • Hand warmers — Reusable gel hand warmers (£2–£5) or disposable warmers can be placed in gloves or pockets

Safety on Ice and Wet Surfaces

  • Wear shoes with good grip — look for deep treads and slip-resistant soles
  • Use walking poles for stability on icy paths
  • Walk on gritted surfaces where possible
  • Take smaller steps to maintain balance
  • Avoid walking after dark when ice is hard to see
  • Slip-on ice grippers for shoes (£5–£15 from outdoor shops) provide extra traction

Warming Up in Cold Weather

Cold muscles and joints need a longer warm-up in winter. Spend 10–15 minutes warming up indoors before heading out: march on the spot, do gentle arm circles, knee lifts and ankle rolls. This increases blood flow to muscles and synovial fluid production before exposing joints to cold temperatures.

Motivation Strategies

  • Schedule exercise — Treat it as an appointment you can't cancel
  • Exercise buddy — Accountability makes you more likely to show up, especially on cold, dark days
  • Midday exercise — Take advantage of daylight during lunch breaks. Even 15 minutes of walking at lunchtime helps
  • Track your activity — Use a simple diary or step counter. Seeing progress is motivating
  • Set winter-specific goals — Rather than comparing to summer activity levels, set realistic winter targets
  • Reward yourself — Plan something enjoyable after exercise: a warm bath, hot chocolate, favourite TV programme
  • Remember the benefits — Exercise improves mood within minutes, and the effects last hours. On the coldest, darkest days, you'll feel the benefit most

Vitamin D in Winter

Between October and March, the UK doesn't receive enough UVB sunlight for vitamin D production. Public Health England recommends all adults take a 10-microgram (400 IU) vitamin D supplement daily during autumn and winter. Vitamin D is important for bone health, immune function and may help reduce arthritis-related inflammation.

Winter doesn't have to mean retreating from physical activity. With the right preparation, indoor alternatives and motivation strategies, you can stay active throughout the British winter and emerge in spring with stronger, more mobile joints. Our virtual assistant can help you create a winter exercise plan tailored to your abilities.

This article is for general information only. Consult your GP before starting a new exercise programme, particularly if you have balance problems or cardiovascular conditions.

Practical next steps for Staying Active with Arthritis in Winter: UK Guide to Cold-Weather Exercise

If you came here about Staying Active with Arthritis in Winter: UK Guide to Cold-Weather Exercise, pick one change you can keep for a fortnight rather than overhauling everything at once. Note what hurts, what helps, and what you have already tried, then take that list to your GP, rheumatology nurse or physiotherapist so the conversation stays concrete.

In many areas you can ask your primary care network about self-referral to physiotherapy or lifestyle support without waiting for a hospital letter. Check your GP surgery website or the NHS App for the route that applies where you live.

Pacing on good and bad days

On better days it is tempting to catch up on everything at once. Spread chores and exercise across the week instead. Use the two-hour rule many physiotherapists suggest: if pain or fatigue is clearly worse two hours after activity, the dose was too high — trim the next session rather than stopping altogether.

Building a joint-friendly routine

Start with short sessions you can repeat on most days. Warm water, cycling, or paced walking often suits stiff joints better than sudden high-impact bursts. Increase time or resistance slowly, and leave a rest day when a joint is hot, swollen or unusually painful. If you are unsure where to begin, ask about NHS physiotherapy or an exercise referral scheme via your GP surgery.

Peer support etiquette

Share what helps you without prescribing it for others. Conditions, medicines and life circumstances differ. If someone is in crisis, encourage them toward NHS 111, their GP, or emergency services rather than relying on a forum alone.

Quick questions about Staying Active with Arthritis

Is this a substitute for seeing a clinician? No. Use it to prepare questions and understand options, then confirm decisions with your NHS team.

How long before I judge whether a change helped? Give most habit or exercise changes at least two to four weeks, unless pain or swelling clearly worsens — in that case scale back sooner.

What should I track? Joint pain (0–10), morning stiffness time, sleep quality, and how far you can walk or how long you can type or stand. Patterns beat one-off ratings.

Safety and when to get urgent help

This page is general information for people in the United Kingdom, not personal medical advice. Seek urgent help via NHS 111 or A&E if you have sudden inability to move a joint, hot swollen joint with fever, chest pain, severe shortness of breath, or symptoms that feel immediately dangerous.
